title: Diamond Open Access for Scholarly Books: Lessons from Croatia
content:
Blog post by Iva Melinščak Zlodi (*)

The possibilities for making research openly accessible, and for enabling authors to retain control over their rights, are closely connected to the scholarly publishing models that dominate in different countries. This connection matters most in countries where resources to cover article and book processing charges (APCs and BPCs) are limited, and where publishing agreements that cover Open Access (OA) fees offer only partial solutions. Croatia offers a useful example of how established non-commercial publishing traditions can support more equitable access to scholarly knowledge.

title: Better Late than Never: Ten Years On, Time to Put the e-Lending Ruling into Law
content:
Ten years ago today, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) determined that a library lending an e-Book is, in law, a library lending a physical book. A decade later, libraries are still waiting for the law to say so. Legislators at EU and national levels have proven stubbornly resistant to efforts to get them to fulfil their obligations to uphold and abide by EU law, encouraged by those who gain from the status quo.

This is not for want of a need for change. Since 2016, the arguments and evidence for a sound and simple legal basis for e-Lending in Europe have kept piling up.

On the 10th anniversary of the Vereniging Openbare Bibliotheken (VOB) vs Stichting Leenrecht judgement, we look back at what the Court said, why it matters, and how the upcoming copyright reform in the EU offers a way to do better for Europe’s researchers, learners, teachers and readers.

The VOB case stemmed from uncertainty in the Netherlands about whether the lending of e-Books could take place under the EU’s existing Rental and Lending Directive.

title: France’s Open Science Strategy: National Ambition, Local Delivery, and AI
content:
Blog post by Camille Françoise and Ophélie Wang

Published in September 2026 and presented by the Ministry of Research, the new French Strategy for Open Science (2026-2033) follows two previous “national plans” for Open Science (OS), dating back to 2018 and 2021. The Strategy spans 100 pages and cites more than 100 publications. It is a reflective text setting out France’s ambitions for OS, offering both a review of nearly ten years of public policy support in this area and an overview of the main priorities for the years ahead.

This article focuses on one key conclusion and one forward-looking perspective from the Strategy, highlighting their potential relevance for other countries in the European context and, more specifically, for the work carried out under the Knowledge Rights 21 (KR21) programme.

The Strategy sets out the challenges that OS still faces and recognises that the barriers remain both strong and diverse: publishing practices and cultures across disciplines, reluctance to share data, lack of funding, and others. These barriers were identified through a survey asking universities and research institutions to name the factors they considered the main hurdles to OS.

title: Save Our Stories: Why Libraries Need the Law on Their Side
content:
Today, 5 November, is World Digital Preservation Day, and this year’s theme, “Save our Stories (SOS): Our digital heritage in danger”, could not be more timely for libraries.

Few missions are more central to libraries than preservation. From local history collections in public libraries to rare books in academic centres and the full national bibliographies held by national libraries, ensuring that the past and present survive into the future is a core role.

Preservation, crucially, is less about an attachment to the past than about an investment in the future. Without it, researchers, communities, and citizens are all the poorer. Access to facts, records and ideas is vital for study, democratic transparency, and the fulfilment of cultural rights.

There are therefore plenty of reasons to be concerned about a 21st-century black hole in library collections that is only getting deeper.

title: Towards Unlocking Spain’s Twentieth-Century Black Hole: Libraries and CEDRO in Dialogue at the LIBER 2026 Conference
content:
Blog post by Ana Ordás
See the Spanish coverage on FESABID’s website.

On 1 October, at the LIBER 2026 conference in Barcelona, FESABID, the Spanish Federation of Archives, Libraries, Museums and Documentation Associations, which serves as the national coordinator for Knowledge Rights 21 (KR21) in Spain, organised the roundtable: “Out-of-commerce works: dialogue between libraries and collective management.”

The session presented publicly, for the first time since late 2025, the state of play of the talks FESABID has held with CEDRO, the Spanish collective management organisation (CMO) for text-based works. The aim is to reach a framework licence agreement for out-of-commerce works.

The speakers were:

  • Antonio Martínez Bodi, from law firm Abogados de las Artes, legal adviser to FESABID in the negotiations;
  • Carolina Santamarina, from FESABID’s Intellectual Property Working Group; and,
  • Javier Díaz de Olarte, representing CEDRO.

    • The session was moderated by Ana Ordás (FESABID, KR21 Spain).

title: Silence Has a Cost: Why Open Advocates Must Answer the Copyright Consultation
content:
Open Access Week may be over for 2026, but the need for advocacy and engagement for sustainable openness continues. If you have any energy left over after all the events, webinars and more, make sure you respond to the European Commission’s targeted consultation on copyright reform!

Much of the success of the Open Access (OA) and Open Science (OS) movements comes from the research sector’s own mobilisation. The readiness of researchers, institutions and funders to opt-out of publishing models based on the exploitation of copyright has had a transformative impact on scholarly communication.

At the same time, researchers use a wide range of content, so open access will only take us so far. Therefore, the value of getting the right conditions and support under national and European law cannot be overstated. Alongside providing funding for OA and OS infrastructures and mandating open publication of publicly supported research, wider laws like copyright are vital.

title: Joint Statement by KR21, ALLEA, LIBER and SPARC Europe: Why Splitting Open Access from the ERA Act Would Cost Researchers
content:
While momentum seems to be building towards the introduction of a Secondary Publication Right (SPR) in EU law, a critical question remains: under which legal framework will this happen?

For years, preparatory work had been taking place as part of the European Research Area (ERA) Policy Agenda, overseen by the part of the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Research and Innovation. This led to well-evidenced reports on the legal barriers to accessing and sharing research, as well as an exploration of the impacts of different potential solutions.

However, in recent months, the suggestion has emerged that rather than being included in the forthcoming ERA Act, SPR should instead be part of a potential copyright reform to be launched in 2027.

This raises concerns. Separating an SPR from efforts to strengthen Open Access mandates risks leaving researchers in a difficult situation, caught between funder expectations, publisher requirements, and limited resources to pay Article Processing Charges. While ‘transformative’ agreements sometimes cover both publication and access costs, these are widely seen as unsustainable.

title: Unifying the Field: Library Advocacy From Greece to Europe
content:
Blog post by Giorgos Glossiotis

The Knowledge Rights 21 (KR21) Let Libraries Be Libraries Action Plan sets out nine asks for EU and national governments, covering licensing terms, contract override, digital locks, out-of-commerce works and education. Pursuing them at the national level takes coalitions, evidence and library associations confident enough to take copyright issues to national policymakers. Two days in Greece on 24 and 25 September focused on building that capacity, around the mid-term meeting of the International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions (IFLA) Europe Regional Division Committee (ERDC).

Day one, 24 September, featured two workshops for ERDC members and guests from the Greek library community, focused on KR21’s initiatives to support libraries in the 21st century. The sessions were led by KR21 representatives Stephen Wyber (Programme Lead/IFLA), Maarten Zeinstra (national coordinator for the Netherlands), and Giorgos Glossiotis (national coordinator for Greece and Cyprus).

title: The Right Thing to Do: How Openness Supports Research Integrity
content:
The theme of International Open Access Week this year is the cost of knowledge. This shines a light both on the major contributions made by the research sector itself (and how these are then captured by private actors) and on the lack of transparency around costs in the publishing field. 

One argument made to justify the continued use of paywalls and high fees for article processing is that this helps to maintain the infrastructure for safeguarding scientific integrity, from peer review to editorial checks and the handling of misconduct. Without these business models, the story goes, these services can no longer be provided. Yet given how little transparency there is on publishing costs, it is rarely clear how much of what institutions and funders pay actually goes towards integrity.

Integrity is indeed a major issue. It is essential not only to maintain the quality of science, but also to safeguard the trust of the public and funders. Stories of malpractice damage confidence in research as a whole. 

The question then is whether closing access (either to reading through subscription fees, or to publishing through article processing charges) is an acceptable ‘sacrifice’.
